---
title: "The models"
---




MINTverse ships four trained models, three gradient-boosted trees in `estimint` that convert
between transmission quantities and one sequence model in `stateMINT` that produces
trajectories. Nothing is fitted, tuned or configured at call time. All you choose is which
model to load and what to put into it.

## The three estiMINT conversions

The three conversions share the same six covariates describing the setting (`dn0_use`, `Q0`,
`phi_bednets`, `seasonal`, `itn_use` and `irs_use`), and differ only in what is converted.

| Name | Extra input | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `"prevalence"` | `prev_y9` | EIR |
| `"hbr"` | `hbr_y9` | EIR |
| `"eir_to_hbr"` | `eir` | HBR |

`load_xgb_model` returns a dictionary rather than a bare booster, because the booster is only
part of the estimator.

::: {#89457f9b .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from estimint import load_xgb_model

model = load_xgb_model("prevalence")

print("features   ", model["features"])
print("transform  ", model["preprocess"]["transform"], "->", model["preprocess"]["inverse"])
print("calibrator ", model["calibrator"]["kind"])
print("rounds     ", model["best_nrounds"])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
features    ['dn0_use', 'Q0', 'phi_bednets', 'seasonal', 'itn_use', 'irs_use', 'prev_y9']
transform   log10 -> pow10
calibrator  qmap+scale
rounds      3382
```
:::
:::


The target is $\log_{10}(\mathrm{EIR})$ rather than EIR, because EIR spans several orders of
magnitude. On the raw scale squared error would be dominated by the high-transmission rows,
while the low end was fitted as noise. Training on the log makes the loss relative, so a
factor-of-two error costs the same at EIR 2 as at EIR 200. `run_xgb_model` inverts the transform
(`pow10`) before returning, so the EIR comes back in natural units.

The quantile-mapping calibrator sits after the booster, because a boosted-tree ensemble regresses
towards the mean. Its predictions come out compressed relative to the truth, most severely in the
tails where the extreme settings are. Quantile mapping puts the marginal distribution of
predictions back onto the distribution of the training targets. That restores the spread the loss
function shrank.

The monotone smoothing pass runs over the calibrated result, because trees are
piecewise-constant. A raw booster predicting EIR from prevalence produces a staircase, flat over
a range of prevalences and then a step, and it can be locally non-monotone, so a slightly higher
prevalence maps to a slightly lower EIR. That is physically wrong. It also prevents any reliable
inversion or optimisation against the model, and the smoothing pass enforces monotonicity along
the input being converted.

Calibration and smoothing are baked into the fitted artefact rather than applied batch-wise
across whatever rows you happen to pass, so a single-row query still lands on a smooth, monotone
curve. Sweep prevalence from 0.05 to 0.75 and the EIRs rise monotonically, on a curve rather than
a staircase.

The models are bundled inside the wheel. Nothing is downloaded, and `load_xgb_model` is a local
file read.

## The stateMINT emulator

`stateMINT` is a Mamba2 state-space model, implemented in JAX and Flax and trained to reproduce
[`malariasimulation`](https://mrc-ide.github.io/malariasimulation/). It takes a setting and a
campaign, and returns 157 steps of prevalence or 157 steps of cases. The architecture is stored
in the artefact and can be read back.

::: {#a4d36e12 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

artifact = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

for key, value in artifact.model_config.items():
    print(f"{key:<12} {value}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
model_type   Mamba2Regressor
predictor    prevalence
input_size   16
d_model      256
n_layers     2
d_state      128
d_conv       4
expand       2
head_dim     64
chunk_size   256
output_dim   1
dropout      0.24
```
:::
:::


The configuration is two layers, `d_model` 256, `d_state` 128, and 16 input channels per
timestep, and those 16 channels are the twelve static covariates, with the `after_intervention`
ones switched on at day 3285, plus the four derived time channels that `prepare_inputs` builds.
It is a small model, which is why it runs comfortably on a CPU.

`from_pretrained` returns a **`ModelArtifact`** rather than a `Mamba2Regressor`, so the network
itself is `artifact.model`, bundled with the scaler and the two config dictionaries. A set of
weights without its scaler is useless. Note that `predictor` is baked into the checkpoint, and
that prevalence and cases are separately trained models with separate scalers. Loading the wrong
one returns a prediction for the other quantity, without any error being raised.

### Causality

The model is **causal**. The prediction at step $t$ depends only on the inputs at steps
$1 \dots t$ and never on anything later, and the architecture enforces this rather than leaving
the training to learn it.

Causality is what makes the pre-campaign baseline meaningful. The `after_intervention`
covariates are zero for every step before day 3285, and the model cannot see forward, so the
first 78 steps are computed as though no campaign were coming. Two scenarios that differ only in
their campaign share an identical baseline, and any difference between their curves is the
campaign.

### Model space and natural units

Prevalence is trained in **logit** space and cases in **log1p** space. Both raw targets are badly
shaped for squared error. A proportion trained directly on 0–1 can be predicted outside its own
bounds, and squared error treats 0.01 against 0.02 as negligible when epidemiologically it is a
doubling. The logit fixes both. Case counts are non-negative and heavily skewed, and `log1p`
handles the zeros that a plain log would not.

`predict` inverts the transform by default. Prevalence comes back in $[0, 1]$ and cases come back
as counts, and passing `transformed=True` returns model space instead, which is what you want
when computing residuals against training targets, on the scale the loss was defined on. It is
almost never what you want when plotting.

::: {.callout-note}
## A note on the word "state"

The *state* in `stateMINT` is the state of a **state-space model**, a hidden vector carried
through a linear recurrence that lets the network summarise everything it has seen up to step
$t$ in fixed memory. `d_state` 128 is the width of that vector.

It is **not** an epidemiological compartment. There is no susceptible, exposed, infected or
recovered class anywhere in the model. The emulator learned a mapping from covariates to
observed trajectories, and never represented the compartmental structure that generated them.
S/I/R dynamics require the simulator.
:::

## See also

The twelve inputs the emulator takes, and the grid they are laid on, are set out in [Covariates
and the time grid](../05-statemint/covariates.qmd), and `predict` in practice in [Calling the
emulator](../05-statemint/the-emulator.qmd). Please see [estiMINT
internals](../07-under-the-hood/estimint-internals.qmd) for the calibration pipeline in full.
